content.text:
What kind of fairy tale is The Frog Prince?

The Frog Prince is the very first story (KHM 1) in the Brothers Grimm collection, where a bond that begins over a golden ball leads to the miracle of a promise kept and a magical transformation. It teaches children ages 4–7 the courage to keep a promise and how to see the heart behind the outward appearance.

content.alt: The Frog Prince - The original Frog Prince story
content.text:
The original Frog Prince story

The original German title is "Der Froschkönig oder der eiserne Heinrich (The Frog King, or Iron Heinrich)," and the Brothers Grimm placed it as the very first story in Volume 1 of their 1812 collection. In the original, the spell is broken not by a kiss but by the princess throwing the frog against the wall, and the moving ending comes when the faithful servant Heinrich's iron bands burst from his chest out of joy.

content.alt: The Frog Prince - A summary of the Frog Prince story
content.text:
A summary of the Frog Prince story

When the youngest princess drops her golden ball into a pond, a frog fetches it back after she promises to be his friend and live with him. The princess forgets her promise and runs away, but the next day the frog appears at the castle gate, and following her father the king's teaching, she keeps her word. The frog transforms into a prince, and the princess, truly sorry for her behavior, sets off on a happy journey together with him.

content.alt: The Frog Prince - The moral of The Frog Prince
content.text:
The moral of The Frog Prince

The heart of it is that a promise must always be kept, and you should look at the heart rather than the outward appearance. It also shows that the courage to admit a mistake and apologize is a virtue in itself. Talk with your child about, "Should you keep a promise even when you don't want to?"

content.alt: The Frog Prince - How to read it aloud to your child
content.text:
How to read it aloud to your child

Read the princess in a prickly voice at first, then in a sincere, heartfelt voice once the frog becomes a prince. Slipping in a "Ribbit, ribbit!" croak here and there makes it even more fun. Pausing for a moment right before the transformation and looking into your child's eyes deepens their engagement. Best suited for ages 4–7.

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Q. What age is The Frog Prince good for?
A. It's best suited for ages 4–7. The plot is clear, and with its distinct themes of promises and sincerity, even children encountering a classic for the first time can easily understand it.

Q. Is the ending different in the original and in picture-book versions?
A. The core (the golden ball, the promise, the transformation) is the same, but in the original the spell is broken by throwing the frog against the wall, and the kiss is a later version. Editions for young children are usually softened in their adaptation.

Q. What kinds of conversations are good to have?
A. Talk together about, "Why is it important to keep a promise?" and "Have you ever judged someone by their appearance alone?"
